claim: Salmonella Dublin is a host-adapted, invasive nontyphoidal Salmonella (iNTS) serovar that causes bloodstream infections in humans.
source: Salmonella Dublin is a host-adapted, invasive nontyphoidal Salmonella (iNTS) serovar that causes bloodstream infections in humans and demonstrates increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of S. Dublin.

claim: Salmonella Dublin demonstrates increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
source: Salmonella Dublin is a host-adapted, invasive nontyphoidal Salmonella (iNTS) serovar that causes bloodstream infections in humans and demonstrates increasing prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: The study analyzed 1303 S. Dublin genomes from a global dataset.
source: Using a global dataset of 1303 genomes, coupled with in vitro assays, we examined the evolutionary, resistance, and virulence characteristics of S. Dublin.
evidence: The dataset size is explicitly stated in the abstract and methods.

claim: Highly resistant S. Dublin isolates are confined predominantly to North America.
source: Our analysis revealed strong geographical associations between AMR profiles and plasmid types, with highly resistant isolates confined predominantly to North America, linked to IncC plasmids co-encoding AMR and heavy metal resistance.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic and resistance data in the results.

claim: Highly resistant North American S. Dublin isolates are linked to IncC plasmids co-encoding AMR and heavy metal resistance.
source: Our analysis revealed strong geographical associations between AMR profiles and plasmid types, with highly resistant isolates confined predominantly to North America, linked to IncC plasmids co-encoding AMR and heavy metal resistance.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by plasmid analysis in the results.

claim: Australian S. Dublin isolates were largely antimicrobial-susceptible.
source: By contrast, Australian isolates were largely antimicrobial-susceptible, reflecting differing AMR pressures.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by resistance profiling data.

claim: Two phylogenetically distinct Australian lineages of S. Dublin were identified: ST10 and ST74.
source: We identified two phylogenetically distinct Australian lineages, ST10 and ST74, with a small number of ST10 isolates harbouring a novel hybrid plasmid encoding both AMR and mercuric resistance.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by phylogenetic analysis.

claim: A small number of Australian ST10 isolates harbour a novel hybrid plasmid encoding both AMR and mercuric resistance.
source: We identified two phylogenetically distinct Australian lineages, ST10 and ST74, with a small number of ST10 isolates harbouring a novel hybrid plasmid encoding both AMR and mercuric resistance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by plasmid sequencing and analysis.

claim: The ST10 lineage remains globally dominant.
source: Whereas the ST10 lineage remains globally dominant, the ST74 lineage was less prevalent.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the phylogenetic distribution data showing 1295 ST10 isolates versus 8 ST74 isolates.

claim: The ST74 lineage was less prevalent than ST10.
source: Whereas the ST10 lineage remains globally dominant, the ST74 lineage was less prevalent.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the phylogenetic distribution data.

claim: ST74 exhibited a larger pan genome compared to ST10.
source: ST74 exhibited unique genomic features including a larger pan genome compared to ST10 and the absence of key virulence loci, including Salmonella pathogenicity island (SPI)-19 which encodes a type VI secretion system (T6SS).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by pangenome analysis data.

claim: ST74 lacks Salmonella pathogenicity island (SPI)-19 which encodes a type VI secretion system (T6SS).
source: ST74 exhibited unique genomic features including a larger pan genome compared to ST10 and the absence of key virulence loci, including Salmonella pathogenicity island (SPI)-19 which encodes a type VI secretion system (T6SS).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by genomic analysis and long-read sequencing data.

claim: The ST74 lineage displayed enhanced intracellular replication in human macrophages compared with ST10.
source: Despite these genomic differences, the ST74 lineage displayed enhanced intracellular replication in human macrophages and induced less pro-inflammatory responses compared with ST10, suggesting alternative virulence strategies that may support systemic dissemination of ST74.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by in vitro infection assays.

claim: The ST74 lineage induced less pro-inflammatory responses compared with ST10.
source: Despite these genomic differences, the ST74 lineage displayed enhanced intracellular replication in human macrophages and induced less pro-inflammatory responses compared with ST10, suggesting alternative virulence strategies that may support systemic dissemination of ST74.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by cytokine and cytotoxicity assays.

claim: The Vi antigen was absent in all ST10 and ST74 genomes.
source: The Vi antigen was absent in all ST10 and ST74 genomes, highlighting challenges for serotyping and vaccine development, and has implications for current diagnostic and control strategies for S. Dublin infections.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by genomic screening for the viaB locus.

claim: Invasive nontyphoidal Salmonella (iNTS) infections are a major cause of global morbidity and mortality.
source: Invasive nontyphoidal Salmonella (iNTS) infections are a major cause of global morbidity and mortality (Stanaway et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: iNTS infections are associated with a relatively limited number of serovars including S. Dublin, S. Panama, S. Virchow, S. Choleraesuis, and S. Typhimurium ST313.
source: Of the >2500 NTS serovars, iNTS infections are associated with a relatively limited number of serovars. These include Salmonella enterica serovar Dublin (S. Dublin), S. Panama, S. Virchow, S. Choleraesuis, and S. Typhimurium ST313 (Parisi et al., 2019; Mughini-Gras et al., 2020; Kingsley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: S. Dublin is a bovine-adapted pathogen.
source: S. Dublin, a bovine-adapted pathogen, is one of the leading iNTS serovars both in Australia and globally (Cheng et al., 2019a; Williamson et al., 2018; Mangat et al., 2019) and is associated with bacteraemia in a high proportion of infections (Parisi et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2019a; Williamson et al., 2018; Mangat et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: S. Dublin is one of the leading iNTS serovars both in Australia and globally.
source: S. Dublin, a bovine-adapted pathogen, is one of the leading iNTS serovars both in Australia and globally (Cheng et al., 2019a; Williamson et al., 2018; Mangat et al., 2019) and is associated with bacteraemia in a high proportion of infections (Parisi et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2019a; Williamson et al., 2018; Mangat et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: S. Dublin is associated with bacteraemia in a high proportion of infections.
source: S. Dublin, a bovine-adapted pathogen, is one of the leading iNTS serovars both in Australia and globally (Cheng et al., 2019a; Williamson et al., 2018; Mangat et al., 2019) and is associated with bacteraemia in a high proportion of infections (Parisi et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2019a; Williamson et al., 2018; Mangat et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Symptomatic cattle may develop septicaemia and transplacental transmission from S. Dublin infection.
source: Symptomatic cattle may develop septicaemia and transplacental transmission (Mangat et al., 2019; Reichel et al., 2018), while asymptomatic infections in cattle enable persistence within the herd population, facilitating disease spread (Mangat et al., 2019; Kirchner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Asymptomatic S. Dublin infections in cattle enable persistence within the herd population, facilitating disease spread.
source: Symptomatic cattle may develop septicaemia and transplacental transmission (Mangat et al., 2019; Reichel et al., 2018), while asymptomatic infections in cattle enable persistence within the herd population, facilitating disease spread (Mangat et al., 2019; Kirchner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: S. Dublin causes zoonotic infections predominately through the consumption of contaminated dairy and meat produce.
source: S. Dublin causes zoonotic infections predominately through the consumption of contaminated dairy and meat produce (McDonough et al., 1999; Davidson et al., 2018; Fenske et al., 2019), and as such is considered a 'One Health' pathogen (McDonough et al., 1999; Davidson et al., 2018; Fenske et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: S. Dublin is considered a 'One Health' pathogen.
source: S. Dublin causes zoonotic infections predominately through the consumption of contaminated dairy and meat produce (McDonough et al., 1999; Davidson et al., 2018; Fenske et al., 2019), and as such is considered a 'One Health' pathogen (McDonough et al., 1999; Davidson et al., 2018; Fenske et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in NTS has increased over the past several decades, leading to the reduction of therapeutic options.
source: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in NTS has increased over the past several decades, leading to the reduction of therapeutic options (Williamson et al., 2018; Sia et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: A multidrug-resistant (MDR) S. Dublin lineage has recently been described in North America, characterised by varying profiles of AMR to ampicillin, streptomycin, chloramphenicol, sulphonamides, tetracyclines, and third-generation cephalosporins (3GC).
source: For example, a multidrug-resistant (MDR; defined as resistance to ≥3 antimicrobial classes [Magiorakos et al., 2012]) lineage has recently been described in North America, characterised by varying profiles of AMR to ampicillin, streptomycin, chloramphenicol, sulphonamides, tetracyclines, and third-generation cephalosporins (3GC).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: MDR S. Dublin isolates all type as sequence type 10 (ST10).
source: These MDR S. Dublin isolates all type as sequence type 10 (ST10), and the AMR determinants have been demonstrated to be carried on an IncC plasmid that has recombined with a virulence plasmid encoding the spvRABCD operon (Mangat et al., 2019; Fenske et al., 2019; Hsu et al., 2019; Mangat et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The AMR determinants in MDR S. Dublin have been demonstrated to be carried on an IncC plasmid that has recombined with a virulence plasmid encoding the spvRABCD operon.
source: These MDR S. Dublin isolates all type as sequence type 10 (ST10), and the AMR determinants have been demonstrated to be carried on an IncC plasmid that has recombined with a virulence plasmid encoding the spvRABCD operon (Mangat et al., 2019; Fenske et al., 2019; Hsu et al., 2019; Mangat et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: S. Dublin is closely related to S. Enteritidis and S. Gallinarum.
source: S. Dublin is closely related to S. Enteritidis and S. Gallinarum (Langridge et al., 2015), with differences in accessory genome content reflective of adaptation to different ecological niches (Langridge et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Differences in accessory genome content between S. Dublin, S. Enteritidis, and S. Gallinarum are reflective of adaptation to different ecological niches.
source: S. Dublin is closely related to S. Enteritidis and S. Gallinarum (Langridge et al., 2015), with differences in accessory genome content reflective of adaptation to different ecological niches (Langridge et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The majority of the sequence types (STs) reported for S. Dublin are ST10 or single-locus variants of this ST.
source: The majority of the sequence types (STs) reported for S. Dublin are ST10 or single-locus variants of this ST, although there is a second lineage, ST74, that is distinct from the main S. Dublin population (Achtman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: ST74 is a second lineage that is distinct from the main S. Dublin population.
source: The majority of the sequence types (STs) reported for S. Dublin are ST10 or single-locus variants of this ST, although there is a second lineage, ST74, that is distinct from the main S. Dublin population (Achtman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The uncommon S. Dublin lineage ST74 may be variably serotyped as S. Dublin or S. Enteritidis dependent upon the strains used to generate typing sera in different laboratories.
source: This uncommon S. Dublin lineage, ST74, may be variably serotyped as S. Dublin or S. Enteritidis dependent upon the strains used to generate typing sera in different laboratories (Achtman et al., 2012), which may have also contributed to it not being identified.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Three non-synonymous point mutations in fliC (Ala220Val, Thr315Ilc, and Thr318Ala) differentiate S. Dublin from S. Enteritidis.
source: The antigenic formula of S. Dublin (1,9,12:g,p:-) is highly similar to S. Enteritidis (1,9,12:g,m:-), with three non-synonymous point mutations in fliC (Ala220Val, Thr315Ilc, and Thr318Ala) differentiating the two serovars.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: The Vi antigen is absent in many S. Dublin isolates.
source: Although the Vi capsular antigen (encoded by the viaB locus) is part of the antigenic definition for S. Dublin, it has been shown that the Vi antigen is absent in many S. Dublin isolates (Achtman et al., 2012; Selander et al., 1992).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Putative virulence determinants in S. Dublin include Salmonella pathogenicity islands (SPIs) 6 and 19, which both encode type VI secretion system (T6SS) machineries.
source: Other putative virulence determinants in S. Dublin include Salmonella pathogenicity islands (SPIs) 6 and 19, which both encode type VI secretion system (T6SS) machineries (Pezoa et al., 2014; Blondel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The presence of two T6SSs in S. Dublin contrasts with other NTS serovars, which encode a single T6SS.
source: The presence of two T6SSs in S. Dublin contrasts with other NTS serovars, which encode a single T6SS (Pezoa et al., 2014; Blondel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: Recent studies have demonstrated a role for SPI-6 and SPI-19 in interbacterial competition by specific S. Dublin strains.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated a role for SPI-6 and SPI-19 in interbacterial competition by specific S. Dublin strains (Blondel et al., 2023; Amaya et al., 2022); however, their effect on host immune processes remains largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation support.

claim: The effect of SPI-6 and SPI-19 on host immune processes remains largely unknown.
source: Recent studies have demonstrated a role for SPI-6 and SPI-19 in interbacterial competition by specific S. Dublin strains (Blondel et al., 2023; Amaya et al., 2022); however, their effect on host immune processes remains largely unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: A total of 1303 S. Dublin genomes were included in the analysis, spanning four decades.
source: A total of 1303 S. Dublin genomes were included in our analysis, spanning four decades (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The dataset included 53 genomes from humans in Australia.
source: This dataset included 53 genomes from humans in Australia, and 1250 genomes from Africa, Europe, North and South America collected from humans (n=462), animals (n=551), food (n=223), and other sources that were not stated (n=67) (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 1235 genomes (99.4%) were ST10 and 58 were a single locus variant (SLV) of ST10.
source: In total, 1235 genomes (99.4%) were ST10 and 58 were a single locus variant (SLV) of ST10, with two double locus variant genomes (e.g. ST4100) restricted to isolates from South America.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: ST74 and SLV ST1545 were only detected in Australia.
source: The exceptions were ST74 and SLV ST1545 that were only detected in Australia (Figure 1C–E, Supplementary file 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: All isolates, including the ST74 lineage, were serotyped in silico as S. Dublin.
source: All isolates, including the ST74 lineage, were serotyped in silico as S. Dublin.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: The ST74 lineage and a single ST10 isolate had codon profiles in fliC of Gly60, Leu138, Ala220, Thr315, and Ala318.
source: However, the ST74 lineage and a single ST10 isolate had codon profiles in fliC of Gly60, Leu138, Ala220, Thr315, and Ala318, in contrast to the remaining ST10 and SLV, which both had a profile of Gly60, Leu138, Val220, Ile315, and Ala318 (the previously described 'Du2' and 'Du1' electrophoretic profiles [Selander et al., 1992], respectively) (Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation support.

claim: Within the ST10 lineage, five clades were identified using Bayesian analysis of population structure (BAPS).
source: Within the ST10 lineage, five clades were identified using Bayesian analysis of population structure (BAPS), inferred from the alignment of 2957 core single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs).
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: Four clades within ST10 were broadly associated with geographical region.
source: Four clades were broadly associated with geographical region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Australian ST10 isolates (n=39) clustered in clade 1.
source: The Australian ST10 isolates (n=39) clustered in clade 1, while isolates from North America were associated with clade 5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Isolates from North America were associated with clade 5.
source: The Australian ST10 isolates (n=39) clustered in clade 1, while isolates from North America were associated with clade 5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The estimated substitution rate for S. Dublin was 1.05×10–7 (95% highest posterior density [HPD]: 1.16×10–7–9.41×10–8).
source: The estimated substitution rate was 1.05×10–7 (95% highest posterior density [HPD]: 1.16×10–7–9.41×10–8), slightly higher than previous estimated mean substitution rates for host-restricted Salmonella serovars (S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi A) but lower than rates reported for host-generalist NTS serovars S. Kentucky and S. Agona (Duchêne et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation support.

claim: The most recent common ancestor (MRCA) for the S. Dublin's global population was inferred to be 1901 (HPD 1878–1924).
source: The most recent common ancestor (MRCA) for the S. Dublin's global population was inferred to be 1901 (HPD 1878–1924), with the MRCA of the different clades and sub-clades largely falling between 1950 and 2000.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on Bayesian phylodynamic analysis.

claim: The MRCA of clade 5 MDR isolates from North America was estimated to be ~1964 (HPD 1952–1974).
source: For example, the MRCA of clade 5 MDR isolates from North America was estimated to be ~1964 (HPD 1952–1974) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2.

claim: The MRCA of the Australian sub-clade was estimated to be ~1967 (HPD 1953–1980).
source: The MRCA of the Australian sub-clade was estimated to be ~1967 (HPD 1953–1980), with the Australian and North American isolates inferred to have an MRCA~1931 (HPD 1914–1947).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on Bayesian phylodynamic analysis.

claim: 51.5% (667/1,295) of S. Dublin genomes had at least one AMR determinant.
source: Overall, 51.5% (667/1,295) of S. Dublin genomes had at least one AMR determinant, with 632/667 (94.8%) isolates classified as MDR.
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: 632/667 (94.8%) isolates with at least one AMR determinant were classified as MDR.
source: Overall, 51.5% (667/1,295) of S. Dublin genomes had at least one AMR determinant, with 632/667 (94.8%) isolates classified as MDR.

claim: MDR S. Dublin was predominantly identified from North American isolates.

claim: The most prevalent AMR determinants were strA-B (n=620), floR (n=556), tet(A) (n=608), and sul2 (n=596).

claim: The only 3GC resistance mechanism detected was blaCMY-2, present in 467/667 (70%) of AMR S. Dublin genomes.

claim: Gold resistance determinants golS and golT were ubiquitous in S. Dublin (n=1302/1303; 99.9%).
source: Gold resistance determinants golS and golT were ubiquitous in S. Dublin (n=1302/1303; 99.9%) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).

claim: The mer operon was frequently associated with the IncC MDR plasmid (90.1%; n=534/593).

source: Three plasmid replicons, namely IncN, IncX1, and IncFII(S), and an MOBF/MOBP relaxase were detected in one of the Australian S. Dublin ST10 genomes from clade 1 (AUSMDU00035676).
evidence: This is stated in the results.

claim: The AUSMDU00035676 plasmid lacked the spv operon.
source: Comparative analysis revealed the AUSMDU00035676 plasmid lacked the spv operon and had low homology to reference IncN and IncX1/IncFII(S) plasmids previously associated with Salmonella (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1E).

claim: The loss of the spv operon may be associated with a less invasive phenotype.
source: The loss of the spv operon may be associated with a less invasive phenotype (Silva et al., 2017).

source: When applied to our S. Dublin dataset, only 11 genomes (n=11/1303; 0.84%) had an index score <0.5.

Typhimurium ST313 (Hammarlöf et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation support.

source: Some putative virulence factors, such as pagN (cell adhesion and invasion [Lambert and Smith, 2008; Folkesson et al., 1999]) and pgtE (virulence [Hammarlöf et al., 2018; Herrero-Fresno et al., 2014]), were found in 1303 (100%, n=1303/1303) and 1302 (99.9%, n=1302/1303) genomes respectively, and no SNPs in the promoter region of pgtE were detected, a mutation previously reported in invasive S. claim: Each ST10 isolate failed to replicate more than twofold over 24 hr in THP-1 cells.
source: Although predicted invasive index scores were higher for the ST10 population (Figure 4B), each isolate failed to replicate more than twofold over 24 hr in THP-1 cells (Figure 5A), whereas isolates within the ST74 population displayed a sustained increase in fold change of intracellular replication, up to eightfold, over 24 hr (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ST74 isolates displayed a sustained increase in fold change of intracellular replication, up to eightfold, over 24 hr in THP-1 cells.
source: Although predicted invasive index scores were higher for the ST10 population (Figure 4B), each isolate failed to replicate more than twofold over 24 hr in THP-1 cells (Figure 5A), whereas isolates within the ST74 population displayed a sustained increase in fold change of intracellular replication, up to eightfold, over 24 hr (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The ST74 population replicated to significantly higher levels in THP-1 macrophages at 9 and 24 hr post-infection compared to the ST10 population.
source: Comparing bacterial growth (CFU/ml) across both sequence types (STs), both lineages were comparable for initial bacterial uptake (Figure 5C); however, the ST74 population replicated to significantly higher levels in THP-1 macrophages at 9 and 24 hr post-infection (hpi) compared to the ST10 population (Figure 5D–F).

claim: 6 out of 11 isolates within the ST10 population replicated more efficiently (up to 10-fold) in HT-29 cells.
source: In contrast to the results obtained in macrophages, we found that 6 out of 11 isolates within the ST10 population replicated more efficiently (up to 10-fold) in HT-29 cells, whereas all 7 isolates within the ST74 population showed minimal replication (up to twofold) over 24 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-C.

claim: All 7 isolates within the ST74 population showed minimal replication (up to twofold) over 24 hr in HT-29 cells.
